title: Chapter 111 — The Pacific
paragraphs: As we glided past the Bashee isles, we emerged at last upon the great South Sea. Were it not for other things, I could have greeted my dear Pacific with uncounted thanks, for now the long prayer of my youth was answered: that serene ocean rolled eastward from me a thousand leagues of blue.

There is some sweet mystery about this sea — no one knows quite what — whose gently awesome stirrings seem to speak of some hidden soul beneath — like those fabled heavings of the Ephesian sod over the buried Evangelist St. John. And it is fitting that over these sea-pastures, wide-rolling watery prairies and Potters' Fields of all four continents, the waves should rise and fall, and ebb and flow unceasingly; for here millions of mixed shades and shadows, drowned dreams, sleepwalkings, reveries — all that we call lives and souls — lie dreaming, dreaming, still; tossing like sleepers in their beds; the ever-rolling waves made so only by their restlessness.

To any meditative Magian rover, this serene Pacific, once seen, must forever after be the sea of his adoption. It rolls the midmost waters of the world, the Indian Ocean and the Atlantic being only its arms. The same waves wash the breakwaters of the newly built Californian towns, planted only yesterday by the most recent race of men, and bathe the faded but still gorgeous skirts of Asiatic lands older than Abraham; while between them all float milky ways of coral islands, and low-lying, endless, unknown archipelagoes, and impenetrable Japans. Thus this mysterious, divine Pacific girdles the world's whole bulk; makes all coasts one bay to it; seems the tide-beating heart of the earth. Lifted by those eternal swells, you cannot help but acknowledge the seductive god, bowing your head to Pan.

But few thoughts of Pan stirred Ahab's brain as, standing like an iron statue at his accustomed place beside the mizzen rigging, with one nostril he unthinkingly sniffed the sugary musk from the Bashee isles (in whose sweet woods mild lovers must be walking), and with the other consciously breathed in the salt breath of the newfound sea — that sea in which the hated White Whale must even then be swimming. Launched at last upon these almost final waters, and gliding toward the Japanese cruising ground, the old man's purpose intensified. His firm lips met like the lips of a vise; the Delta of his forehead's veins swelled like overloaded brooks; even in his sleep, his ringing cry ran through the vaulted hull: "Stern all! The White Whale spouts thick blood!"
